analysis.one_liner: Lets states make lenders' liens on farm tools, livestock, and crops survive bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee; it had drawn 8 cosponsors, 6 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let states opt to protect lenders' liens on a bankrupt debtor's tools of the trade, implements, animals, and crops from being wiped out, but only in states that pass a law barring debtors from voiding those liens. The sponsors pitched it as a way to make secured farm credit easier to get. It never got a hearing and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Lenders holding security interests in farm equipment, livestock, and crops — chiefly farm and agricultural credit lenders — would keep those liens even when a debtor files for bankruptcy, in any state that adopts the rule. Borrowers might find it easier to borrow against those assets because lenders would face less risk of losing their lien in bankruptcy, but the direct beneficiary is the creditor.

how_it_helps.text: A lender with a nonpossessory, nonpurchase-money lien on a debtor's tools of the trade, implements, animals, or crops could keep that lien in bankruptcy, even though the property would otherwise be exempt from creditors, so long as state law bars the debtor from avoiding the lien.

By making such liens enforceable in bankruptcy, the bill aimed to reassure lenders who make loans secured by farm tools, animals, and crops, which the sponsors argued would improve the availability of secured credit.

analysis.who_pays: Farmers and other debtors who file for bankruptcy. Under current law they can wipe out liens on exempt property such as work tools, animals, and crops; under this bill they could lose those assets to lenders in states that adopt the rule, leaving them without the equipment or stock they need to earn a living.

drawbacks.text: A farmer or tradesperson in financial distress could no longer clear a lender's lien on the very tools, animals, or crops needed to make a living — losing a bankruptcy protection every debtor currently holds.
The rule would apply only where a state passes a matching law, so protection would depend on where a debtor lives, creating a patchwork of state-by-state rules.
The claimed benefit — easier secured credit — is a prediction, while the cost would be immediate and fall on the most financially distressed debtors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated upside is speculative: lenders might extend more credit if their liens are safer in bankruptcy, and the bill only takes effect in states that choose to opt in. The downside is concrete: distressed debtors would lose the ability to protect the tools, animals, and crops they live on, exactly when bankruptcy law is meant to give them a fresh start. On balance the bill trades a real loss for struggling farmers in exchange for an unproven gain in lending.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee without a hearing or vote and expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Sarpalius of Texas introduced the bill on February 5, 1992, joined at introduction by three Texas colleagues.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and on February 11, 1992 it was sent to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law.
No hearing, markup, or vote followed, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bankruptcy debtors came out ahead: they kept the existing protection that lets them wipe out liens on tools, animals, and crops. Farm lenders, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

for.name: Reps. De La Garza, Stenholm, and Combest
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 8 House members
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no committee or floor action ever followed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 5, 1992, and took no action on it.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 11, 1992; no hearing or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 6 Democratic and 2 Republican cosponsors — but no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Liens on tools, implements, animals, and crops would survive bankruptcy in states that opt in, making loans secured by farm assets safer for lenders to make. The gain comes directly out of what distressed farm debtors can keep, so the industry's interest runs against the borrowers it lends to.

industries.industry: Other secured lenders holding liens on work tools
industries.note: The bill covers any nonpossessory, nonpurchase-money lien on tools of the trade, not only farm property, so finance lenders holding such liens would also benefit where states adopt the rule — again at the expense of bankrupt debtors.
